unit.title: Excretion
unit.blurb: Why the body must excrete waste, what urine contains, the parts of the excretory system and how the kidneys filter blood.

O1.t: Explain what excretion is and name the lungs, skin and kidneys as excretory organs.

O2.t: Describe what urine contains and how it changes with water intake.

O3.t: Identify the kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra and describe the path of urine.

O4.t: Describe how the kidneys filter blood, and how dialysis and transplants help when kidneys fail.

captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was written by the Atomic teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 2: Excretion.
Your body is about 60% water.
You can survive around three weeks without food,
but only about three days without water!
We lose water when we sweat and when we use the toilet.
Which organs keep the right amount of water in our bodies?
To excrete means to get rid of.
Excretion removes waste products made by metabolism,
the chemical reactions that keep our cells alive.
It stops toxic substances from building up.
Three main organs excrete.
The lungs remove carbon dioxide and water vapour when we breathe out.
The skin removes water, salts and a little urea in sweat.
And the kidneys remove excess water, salts and urea in urine.
Urea is made when our body breaks down proteins.
Eating more protein than we need increases the amount of urea we must excrete.
A mirror has been kept in a fridge so it is cold.
A student breathes out gently onto it.
Predict: what will appear on the mirror?
Pause and decide.
Watch. The student breathes out slowly onto the cold glass.
A misty patch appears.
Up close, it is made of tiny droplets of water, which slowly disappear.
Explain what you saw.
Breathed-out air contains water vapour, made in our cells by respiration.
When it touches the cold mirror, it condenses into droplets.
So the lungs excrete water vapour as well as carbon dioxide:
they are excretory organs.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Urine is about 95% water.
The other 5% is roughly 2% urea and 3% salts and uric acid.
These figures are only approximate.
Drink a lot of water and your urine becomes paler and you urinate more often.
If you're dehydrated, your body conserves water, so you make less urine,
and it's darker yellow.
These are typical amounts of water lost in one
day by an adult in a cool climate,
who is not exercising hard.
Most water, about one and a half litres, leaves in urine.
About half a litre is lost as sweat,
and almost half a litre in the air we breathe out.
Pause and decide: which of these amounts would rise on a hot day,
and how would the kidneys respond?
The excretory system is made up of two kidneys in the lower back,
two ureters, the bladder and the urethra.
The renal artery and renal vein connect the kidneys to the blood supply.
Urine flows down the ureters and is stored in the bladder.
When it's full, you feel the need to urinate:
a muscle opens and urine leaves through the urethra.
Fun fact: wetlands filter water just like kidneys filter blood!
Blood enters each kidney through the renal artery.
The kidney filters out urea, excess water and excess salts to form urine.
Clean blood, with its useful nutrients, leaves through the renal vein.
Healthy kidneys filter about 180 litres of fluid a day!
If they fail, patients may need dialysis, where a machine cleans their blood,
or a kidney transplant.
We can live with one kidney,
and bioartificial kidneys may be ready by 2030.
Our excretory organs work all day.
Here are four ways they affect everyday life.
During a long run you sweat a lot.
Your kidneys save water, so you make less urine and it is darker.
Pale, straw-coloured urine is a simple sign that you are drinking enough water.
If the kidneys fail,
a dialysis machine filters urea and extra water out of the patient's blood,
several times a week.
A person can live a healthy life with only one kidney,
so a living donor can give a kidney to a patient.
Healthy kidneys keep water, salts and waste in balance.
Pause and think: what colour should your urine be when you are well hydrated?
Now it is your turn to shine!
Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: Name the three main organs of excretion.
Pause the video now.
Answer: Lungs, skin and kidneys.
Question 2: What is urine mostly made of?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Water, about 95%.
Question 3: Which tube carries urine from the kidney to the bladder?
Pause the video now.
Answer: The ureter.
Question 4: Why might your urine be dark yellow?
Pause the video now.
Answer: You are dehydrated, so it contains less water.

adv.prompt: * Advanced. The concentration of urea is 0.4 g/dm³ in blood plasma and 20 g/dm³ in urine. How many times more concentrated is urea in urine than in blood plasma?
adv.reason: 20 ÷ 0.4 = 50 times. The kidneys filter urea out of the blood and reabsorb most of the water.

adv.prompt: * Advanced. NIDDK explains that each kidney has about a million nephrons: a filter (glomerulus) removes water and small substances from the blood, and a tubule returns the substances the body needs. The kidneys filter about 180 litres of fluid a day but make only about 1.5 litres of urine. Calculate the percentage of the filtered fluid that is returned to the blood, and explain why this return is essential.

rubric.pt: needed substances such as glucose, water and useful salts are returned
otherwise we would lose huge amounts of water / dehydrate quickly

adv.model: (180 − 1.5) ÷ 180 × 100 ≈ 99 %, so about 99 % of the filtered fluid is returned to the blood. The tubules return water, glucose and useful salts; without this we would lose about 180 litres of water a day and would quickly become dehydrated and die.
